Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) have emerged as a robust solution for unsupervised learning, offering superior generative capabilities compared to conventional autoencoders. However, their reconstructive performance lags behind that of traditional models. This study introduces a straightforward yet effective approach to enhance the reconstructive efficiency of VAEs by integrating a skip connection within the decoder framework. This addition facilitates a more faithful reconstruction of input data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this method can be seamlessly applied to a range of popular VAE architectures without incurring any increase in model complexity or the number of trainable parameters.

The rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) has introduced significant security challenges, prompting research into blockchain technology as a secure solution. While public blockchains offer strong security, their requirement for extensive computational resources and power makes them ill-suited for IoT environments. In contrast, private blockchains, which are controlled by a single entity or a restricted group of participants, can efficiently operate within homes. This paper examines the potential of utilizing blockchain technology to enhance security in IoT-enabled smart homes. We outline the specific benefits private blockchains offer over public alternatives, focusing on their ability to function with limited resources. Furthermore, the study reviews the current state of smart home architectures and proposes a novel, blockchain-integrated framework designed to bolster overall home security.

This paper introduces a deep learning (DL)-based framework for generating optimized lookup tables (LUTs) designed to enhance the quality of reconstructed data. Our approach utilizes a neural network to generate log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) from a limited set of soft information bits, thereby significantly reducing storage requirements for traditional lookup tables. To ensure the resilience of this method against storage constraints, we developed a GAN-driven pre-training scheme that generates high-quality lookup tables even with minimal deep learning data. Furthermore, we implemented a dynamic quantization technique that stores these generated LUTs via the precise weights of the neural network, achieving superior data reconstruction quality with a 90% reduction in memory usage compared to standard 8-bit quantization.

An upward planar drawing represents the vertices and edges of an acyclic directed graph on the plane using straight lines, adhering to their orientation constraints. This paper introduces a linear-time algorithm capable of generating such drawings for general up-planar graphs, provided they are given a specific input format. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this linear-time approach can be extended to compute optimal embeddings for these up-planar graphs in constant space. An optimal embedding minimizes the vertical height of the resulting drawing. We establish the linear-time computability and linear-space executability of our general up-planar recognition algorithm, which also applies to up-planarity testing under the same resource constraints. Finally, we prove that the problem of recognizing up-planarity in the context of directed cubic planar graphs is linear-time solvable within linear space complexity.

Crowd-sourced image collections are frequently noisy, containing substantial amounts of irrelevant data that hinders the use of standard, fully supervised deep learning models. While current methods to address this rely on either complex, data-intensive semi-supervised algorithms or complex complex co-training methods, the challenge of identifying and filtering this irrelevant data remains unsolved. This paper introduces a new unsupervised method that not only filters noise but also yields a higher-quality training set. By applying a co-occurrence matrix to capture semantic relationships within the dataset, the proposed approach first filters out irrelevant images and then filters a classifier that leverages these newly discovered associations. Experimental results demonstrate that this classifier achieves performance comparable to semi-supervised methods while requiring fewer assumptions and less data.

This study establishes a non-uniform spectral gap for transfer operators applied to smooth observables in uniformly expanding semiflows, where the decay is measured in the Hölder norm. For any such flow, we derive a transfer operator acting on a Banach space of uniformly continuous functions; this operator exhibits Hölder spectral properties with a geometric convergence rate determined by the rate at which Hölder norms decay. Under uniform expansion, we prove that transfer operators admit exponential decay rates in Hölder norms, with spectral gaps expressible as functions of the Hölder continuity constants and exponents of admissible test functions. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these spectral results yield quantitative estimates for mixing rates and decay of correlations.

A covering array, denoted as $[N]_t(M;N)$, is defined as an $M \times N$ array with entries drawn from an alphabet of size $N$, where every possible $N \times N$ subarray contains every possible tuple at least once. This paper establishes sufficient conditions ensuring that a specific random construction of covering arrays of size $N \times N$ over an alphabet of size $N$ is identical to a corresponding Latin square. Applying this framework yields a new, straightforward proof for the existence of randomized Latin squares within any given covering array. Furthermore, the findings are extended to the case of pairwise orthogonal Latin squares under similar conditions.

We introduce a class of nonlocal games where the presence of noise in maximally entangled states can be identified through the optimal success probability achieved by players. Additionally, for the specific cases examined, the measurements employed by the players enable the quantification of a broader class of noisy entangled states by establishing a complete one-to-one relationship between the success probability and the state itself.

Although numerous studies have examined the efficacy of crash reproduction techniques, few directly compare them. This work evaluates and contrasts two such methods: EvoCrash, a widely adopted open-source framework, and JCHARMING, a newly introduced proprietary tool. The comparison centers on their ability to induce software failures within a test suite of 100 open-source projects. Our results indicate that both systems successfully targeted and triggered bugs from the JCHARMING dataset using the new tool and EvoCrach with a success rate of 90.1%. However, EvoCrach demonstrated superior performance in reproducing crashes from the broader set of ten projects analyzed, achieving a 68.8% success rate compared to JCHARMING's 56.8%. Additionally, EvoCrach required fewer iterations to achieve crash reproduction and completed the process more rapidly.

We investigate the magnetic field dependence of the vortex lattice in La$_{2-x}$Sr$_x$CuO$_4$ at zero doping level using small-angle neutron scattering. At temperatures below 20 K, a crossover emerges from an isotropic state to an anisotropic one as the magnetic field increases. This transition occurs at a critical field $B^*$, which rises with decreasing temperature. This behavior is interpreted through a modified melting scenario, where $B^*$ marks the shift from a liquid vortex phase to a vortex crystal. The variation of $B^*$ aligns with a melting process driven by vortex interactions dominated by a repulsive component. Additionally, we observe a weak angular dependence in the intensity of the scattering peak near $B^*$, suggesting a complex phase transition involving both melting and a change in lattice symmetry.

The primary goal of A/B testing is to determine if an A/T Effect (ATE) exists, yet many firms struggle with detecting it. While larger sample sizes can improve detection, they often incur excessive costs and delays. Consequently, companies are increasingly adopting adaptive experiments that sample more heavily when initial results indicate a potential effect. However, these adaptive designs can introduce biases into the A/T Effect estimate and its detection. This study examines the challenges of estimating and detecting the A/T Effect within such adaptive experiments. We introduce a t-test variant for the continuous metric case and a logistic test for binary metrics, both of which account for adaptive experimentation. We also evaluate these approaches through simulations and a real-world case study. Finally, we discuss the practical implementation of these tests in continuous and binary scenarios.
The foundational aspects of cosmological inflation are examined, with emphasis on the dynamics of the inflaton field, the slow-roll approximation, and the generation of primordial fluctuations.

We present findings from CDF II utilizing 192 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV with the CDF II detector at Fermilab. We measured the mass of the W boson by analyzing final states containing a charged lepton and missing transverse momentum, corresponding to a W boson decaying into a lepton-nu pair. Our results yielded a W boson mass measurement of 80.433 $\pm$ 0.040 (stat) $\pm$ 0.035 (sys) GeV. This value exhibits a 7$\sigma$ deviation from Standard Model predictions.

Software developers often struggle to identify suitable search terms when addressing functional changes in software engineering. To overcome this difficulty, we introduce a system that automatically generates functional synsets for Java methods, leveraging the semantic relationships between concepts to organize related terms for shared meanings. By generating these organized search term lists for each method, we enable users to easily identify appropriate search strings without manual effort. We evaluated this approach using a study with 100 real-world search queries from 88 actual developers. The results indicate that our generated synsets were rated as more effective for term discovery than synsets built by a reference system using the same data. Furthermore, when comparing the reference system's single-term searches against a proposed hybrid system that incorporates our synsets, we observed that the hybrid system significantly improved the discovery rate of relevant terms.

Entrainment, defined as the reciprocal alignment of head movements, gestures, and vocal features during social engagement, serves as a critical indicator of rapport and engagement. This study investigates the acoustic characteristics of entrainment in both spontaneous dialogues and controlled tasks, utilizing metrics of convergence (the narrowing of acoustic properties) and lagged synchrony. Results indicate that entrainment occurs in acoustic dimensions beyond just voice pitch, with the balance of synchrony versus convergence shifting based on the experimental context. Furthermore, while interpersonal pitch convergence is a reliable marker of rapport, its predictive value for future alignment events diminishes over time. These findings underscore the necessity of incorporating temporal dynamics when assessing entrainment and offer a foundation for developing future models capable of forecasting these alignments.

We introduce a new repository of spectral energy distributions (SEDs) for 1,000 galaxies, derived from the 100 largest samples available in existing literature. These galaxies span a wide range of redshifts (0 < z < 4) and are characterized by their redshift, luminosity, and star formation rate. Our collection covers a wide spectrum of wavelengths, from 0.3 to 2.5 micrometers, encompassing both near-infrared and far-UV data. We have developed a novel algorithm to generate synthetic observations from these SEDs, simulating data across various wavelengths and resolutions to mimic the output of current and future observatories. This includes simulated outputs resembling the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT). By offering this extensive dataset, our resource can significantly aid in validating galaxy modeling codes, testing statistical methods, and preparing researchers for data analysis using upcoming observational facilities.

Action segmentation involves identifying temporal patterns of human activities within video data. We introduce SSCAP, an unsupervised method that segments videos by analyzing action variations, effectively extracting meaningful information from raw data without annotation. Our approach is model-agnostic, rendering it independent of specific feature extractors and compatible with various visual representations. Evaluations across three datasets demonstrate SSCAP's superior performance compared to other leading unsupervised techniques.

This study investigates the possible existence of $\bar D^{(*)} \Sigma_c^{(*)}$ hadronic molecular states, identifying them as potential $D^*_c(3120)$ and $D^*_c(3160)$ candidates. Utilizing QCD sum rules within the framework of twice-repeated heavy-quark effective theory, we calculate their masses, determining that these negative mass values indicate a stable configuration consistent with a $\bar D^*_c(3120)$ resonance matching the observed $D^*_c(3120)$ mass, while $\bar D^c(3160)$ remains disfavored. Furthermore, we evaluate the decay dynamics of $\bar D^*_c(3120)$ into $D^*_c(3120)\pi$ and $D^*_c(3120)\rho$ channels, finding that the former proceeds predominantly through the $D^*_c(3120)\pi$ mode.

This paper presents the outcomes of a two-year, two-semester educational testing curriculum grounded in test usage investigations. These testing activities encourage students to derive testing principles from empirical observations of testing execution. The course design integrates IEEET's Code of Ethics alongside two distinct inquiry methodologies: K-12-inspired question-driven investigation and data science-oriented hypothesis testing. Over two semesters, students analyzed datasets generated by executing tests across diverse software systems. They employed question-driven inquiry to uncover the connection between testing coverage levels and the probability of detecting faults, whereas exposure to hypothesis testing within the data science framework enabled them to identify the statistical significance of observed correlations. The study evaluates both the pedagogical advantages and limitations of these approaches, reporting positive findings from student and faculty surveys. Furthermore, the paper details the specific testing exercises and materials developed to support this instructional strategy.

Domain Adaptation (DA) addresses the challenge of adapting to an unlabeled target domain when source domain data is available. This work introduces Semi-Supervised Mutual Enhancement (MUSE), a novel DA framework that leverages both unsupervised domain alignment and semi-suppressive supervision. MUSE operates through two primary modules: first, a Semi-Supervised Enhancement (SSE) module that utilizes enhanced pseudo-labels to facilitate accurate classification; second, a Semi-Supervised Domain Enhancement (DSE) module that utilizes classified data to refine feature extraction capabilities. Empirical evaluations on four standard benchmarks demonstrate that MUSE achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing existing methods. The approach is simple, effective, and easy to implement.

A Gas Core Reactor (GCR) is a type of nuclear fission power system that utilizes the gas-phase transport of fuel and a solid control structure, often called a "grain," to modulate the reaction. Within this design, the gas carries enriched Uranium-235 and depleted Uranium-238, forming the active fuel mixture, while the solid grain provides essential neutron reflection and a pathway for gamma radiation. This paper introduces a simplified analytical model designed to calculate the power output of such reactors. The derived formula for the GCR's electrical power output is the product of three specific components: the thermal power generated by the core, the fraction of that heat transferred to the surrounding coolant, and the efficiency with which the Stirling engine converts the resulting thermal energy into electricity. This model is then applied to a proposed GCR concept, the "Tiger," which is a conceptual design for a space-based nuclear power source.

We introduce a novel approach for identifying the interaction location of charged particles within a silicon pixel detector, leveraging a domain-informed neural network (DiNN) that incorporates geometric information and a specialized activation function rooted in the physical distribution of single-hit signals. This physical insight allows the DiNN to surpass standard multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) in both estimating precision and sample efficiency. Furthermore, the DiNN demonstrates robustness against variations in operating conditions, such as changes in incident particle rates or sensor bias voltages, because it is grounded in the fundamental physics governing silicon signal distributions.

We introduce a new approach to generate synthetic spectra for substellar atmospheres, which relies on a parametric model of absorption cross-sections. By utilizing these parameters, we can quickly create numerous synthetic spectra, allowing us to explore how variations in molecular absorption properties influence spectral outcomes. These generated spectra are then compared against our established synthetic spectra, a standard model atmosphere code, and actual observational data. Our findings indicate that the synthetic spectra are in excellent agreement with both the model and observations, demonstrating that the method accurately reproduces the absorption features of H$_2$O, CH$_4$, and NH$_3$ across a wide range of atmospheric conditions.

We introduce a generalized, well-founded-based grounding algorithm that effectively handles programs containing inductive, infinitary definitions. This approach extends the CHANON ground-evaluated operator, a framework well-suited for answering set programming (ASP) programs. We demonstrate that, under well-founded constraints, our proposed operator converges to a semantics equivalent to the standard ASP interpretation. Furthermore, we provide a well-founded version of the CHANON operator to define the semantics for general definitional programs. This operational definition proves to be a valuable tool for analyzing program behavior, particularly in cases involving inductive and infinitary rules.

This study introduces a unified framework for quantum resource theories, addressing scenarios involving multiple resources. In such contexts, a single set of free operations is defined by its interaction with various invariant sets within the state space. Using this formalism, we establish that the free-relative entropy associated with each specific invariant set serves as a universal measure for quantifying the corresponding quantum resource. Furthermore, the invariance of these measures under all free operations and their monotonicity under such operations are demonstrated. We also show that when relative entropy is composed across different invariant sets, it yields a set of free operations characterized by the intersection of those compositions. Finally, our results are applied to the resource theory of quantum coherence, where we derive explicit formulas for the coherent relative entropy relative to the intersection of the stabilizer sets.

Low-density parity-check quantum error-correcting codes are highly desirable due to their efficient implementation of syndrome measurements and the availability of powerful classical decoding algorithms. This paper introduces a novel LDPC code featuring a cyclic structure, characterized by a constant code rate and a uniform code degree distribution. We demonstrate that this code can be constructed from a tiling pattern composed of two distinct hexagons. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive classification of all self-dual variants of this cyclic LDPC code.

In a graph $G=(V,E)$, a subset $D \subseteq V$ constitutes a distance-$r$ dominating set if the shortest path distance from any node in $V \setminus D$ to $D$ is at most $r$. The graph's distance-$r$ domination number, denoted $\gamma_r(G)$, represents the minimum size of such a set. This paper addresses the computational complexity of determining $\gamma_r$ for specific graph families and investigates the parameterized complexity of the distance-$r$ dominating set problem. We demonstrate that finding a minimum distance-$r$ dominating set in interval graphs is NP-hard for every $r \ge 1$. Furthermore, we establish that the problem is fixed-parameter tractable (fpt) when parameterized by $r$ for various graph classes, including interval graphs, chordal bipartite graphs, and permutation graphs.

This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the bulk-boundary correspondence within the context of the gapped $2\text{D}$ higher-order topological insulator (HOTI) square lattice model. We demonstrate that while corner states are generally considered robust, they are in fact protected by the surrounding 1D topological insulator (1DTI) bulk, meaning they can be eliminated by sufficient disorder. Consequently, the stability of these corner states is contingent upon the preservation of the1DTI bulk, a property that also renders them non-stable under certain non-Hermitian conditions. Furthermore, we identify that the 1DTI bulk can be replaced by specific symmetry constraints, leading to the 1DTI's absence and the subsequent symmetry protection of the corner states. Finally, we establish that the stability of these corner states is contingent upon various types of bulk symmetries, including chiral, mirror, and time-reversal symmetries.

This study reports a search for heavy gluinos within the $s\bar t$ supersymmetry model, utilizing data from proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV collected by the CMS experiment at the LHC during 2016–2018. The analysis focuses on events characterized by two b-tagged jets, two or more heavy-flavor jets, large missing transverse momentum, and either two or no isolated leptons alongside a large dijet mass. The observed data aligns with predicted background levels across all considered final states. Consequently, at a 95% confidence level, the study excludes gluino masses up to 1.0 TeV for a scalar top quark mass of 1.5 TeV.

We introduce a four-dimensional light field model trained to generate new views from a single image and a motion field, applicable to both rigid and deformable geometries. This approach offers high-resolution, smooth output across extended time intervals and supports arbitrary camera trajectories. We further demonstrate its capability to synthesize three-dimensional representations, specifically through depth estimation and Gaussian splatter scenes.

We present high-precision, long-baseline optical and near-infrared astrometry for the compact close binary system V471 Tau, acquired using the Very Large Telescope Interferometer's VLTI/GRAVITY instrument. This system exhibits a compact orbit with a period of 2.9 days and a mass ratio of approximately 0.4. By applying VLTI/GRAVy astrometry, we achieve sub-milliarcsecond (mas) precision in the determination of both the relative and barycentric orbits. The resulting barycentric solution demonstrates a precision of 0.3 mas, which is a 1.5-fold improvement over the previously available data. Furthermore, we successfully detect the orbital wobble of the binary system induced by a third companion, designated V471 Tau C, located at a separation of 1.4 arcseconds. The astrometric residuals from the solution reveal a significant wobble with an amplitude of 1.5 mas at a period of 11.5 years, consistent with the orbit of companion C predicted by previous radial velocity studies.

We demonstrate that the difference between the self-dual and anti-self-dual sectors of the self-conjugate Weyl tensor in self-dual gravity corresponds to a specific class of self-dual gravitons. This class of gravitons is defined by the property that their double copy yields the self-dual Weyl tensor. By utilizing this finding, we derive the self-dual portion of one-loop MHV amplitudes for gravity and generalize our approach to the classical field level. This method also facilitates a fresh examination of self-dual Yang-Mills theory, resulting in a generalization of the Berends-Giele recursion to the domain of single gluons. This recursion enables a systematic construction of self-dual multi-gluon amplitudes. Furthermore, we establish that the algebra of area-preserving diffeomorphisms governs both self-dual Yang-Mills theory and self-dual gravitons, playing a pivotal role in the color-kinematics duality.

Solar flares and coronal mass ejections (CMEs) are frequently linked to the occurrence of type II radio bursts, which are generated by shock waves. Although these events are often connected, the precise relationship between the two remains unclear. This study investigates the correlation between flares/CMEs and shock-driven type II radio bursts by analyzing 11 instances identified by the Radio Solar Observatory Network (RSO/N) using data from the Radio Solar Spectrograph (RSSP) aboard the Solar Dynamics and Volcanic Observatory (SDVO). We cross-reference RSSP radio burst timings with Rastered Imaging of X-rays and Gamma Rays (RISG) flare records and Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO) and Advanced Composition Explorer (ACE) CME observations. We find that 10 out of 11 bursts originated from the shock fronts of CMEs, with only one showing a clear flare-burst sequence. We also observe that these CME-associated shocks consistently form bow shocks. These observations indicate that shocks produced by flares or CMEs generate type II radio bursts, but only those driven by CME bow shocks show a consistent correlation.

Our analysis indicates that this framework effectively accounts for several observed anomalies in charged and neutral decays. Specifically, it addresses the discrepancies in $B \to D^{(*)}\ell\nu$ and $B \to \tau\nu$ channels, as well as the $\bar{B}_s$ lifetime anomalies. This study introduces a new framework for defining conditional distributions of point processes, establishing an interpretation for the evolution of vortex rings under mutual induction. We demonstrate that the conditional distributions for random vortex dynamics possess a specific property: the conditional distributions of vortices at a later future moment $t_2$, given vortices at an earlier time $t_1$, are dual to those evolved backward from $t_1$ to a prior moment $t_0$. This result relies on a novel dual distribution principle applicable to point processes generally. The framework finds a specific application in the dynamics governing random vortex loops. Furthermore, we establish an interpretation for random loop measures previously defined by Aizenman and Zlatoš, linking them to conditional distributions of point processes. This dual distribution approach also enables a fresh perspective on random loop measures and provides methods for generating them.

Boson sampling is a quantum optical experiment designed to demonstrate quantum supremacy, where the outcome distribution reflects the squared absolute values of bosonic mode overlaps with specific basis states. In this study, we examine the system's behavior by modeling the linear subspace spanned by these basis states as a qubit ensemble and employing the concept of relative entropy to quantify the distance between the experimental output distribution and an ideal uniform distribution. This approach allows us to define a degree of non-uniformity in the results. By incorporating single-phaser states and considering the subspace dimensions alongside the qubit ensemble structure, we derive an analytical framework for the entropy of the experimental distribution. Our findings reveal that the entropy increases with the count of input modes and the dimension of the subspace, reaching its maximum when both factors are maximized. Furthermore, we establish that the entropy is bounded below by the dimension of the subspace divided by the dimension of the full space. These insights offer a critical foundation for the quantitative characterization of the experimental distribution.

By extending the unsupervised STTM model, SGT-TT enables the classification of continuous temporal sequences into distinct states. The unsupervised foundation of SGT-TT stems from its ability to project high-dimensional data onto a two-dimensional surface while maintaining local neighborhood relationships. The model's temporal dimension is expanded to capture sequence patterns, which are then differentiated using a supervised learning framework. Reinforcement learning (RL) agents often face challenges in learning effective policies due to the high variance in Bellman updates. Although recent research has introduced low-variance estimators, these estimators can still yield high mean squared error (MSE) when sample sizes are small. We propose a method that leverages recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to forecast future outcomes, thereby enhancing the expected return of RL agents by reducing bias in value function estimation through historical context. We further demonstrate that combining this approach with variance-reduction techniques yields substantial performance gains.

Detecting spatiotemporal actions in video is a highly challenging yet essential task, as these activities are defined by their location within a scene, the entities involved, and the temporal evolution of their interactions. Current state-of-the-art methods often overlook these critical aspects, instead relying on the assumption that action classes are strongly correlated with visual features derived from raw pixels. This paper introduces a new approach to spatiotemporal action detection that explicitly models actions based on their spatial context, the behavior of individual agents, and the dynamics of their relationships. Our method integrates a specialized feature set that combines human-centric body part annotations with motion dynamics extracted from skeleton data. Furthermore, we employ a novel attention mechanism to automatically weigh the significance of each feature within an action class. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art results on the MakeMeMine-Youtube dataset and demonstrates competitive performance on the UCF101 dataset. The source code can be accessed at: https://github.com/rohitgarg00/Spatial-Temporal-Action-Detection.

Detecting and removing human manipulations from images is a critical yet difficult challenge with significant real-world applications. While current state-of-the-art methods focus on supervised learning using human-analysed transformations, they often fail to generalize to unsupervised scenarios. To address this, we introduce a novel framework for automatically generating image transformations without human intervention. Our method creates a substantial dataset of unsupplied transformed images by leveraging image editing tools and computer vision algorithms. We identify three key factors that determine transformation difficulty: (1) the necessity of domain-specific knowledge, (2) the lack of a standardized evaluation metric, and (3) the scarcity of annotated transformation data. Using this auto-generated dataset, we train a copy-detection model that achieves superior performance in both supervised and zero-shot generalization scenarios compared to existing approaches.

This study examines diffusion processes that exhibit metastability when the parameter $\varepsilon$ approaches zero, focusing on the impact of random noise confined to a bounded region of small magnitude. Specifically, the authors derive the logarithmic asymptotics of the mean exit time required for the process to reach the noise-free complement beyond a noise-affected window, considering regimes where both global and local metastability phenomena are present.

This study examines the influence of both weak and strong magnetic fields on the spin polarization of nuclear matter, employing the relativistic mean-field framework. We analyze the behavior of the total spin polarization as a function of both magnetic field strength and density. Our results indicate that the total spin polarization increases with rising both density and the magnitude of the applied magnetic field. Additionally, we observe that the spin polarization remains invariant for neutrons and varies only slightly for protons across different magnetic field strengths.

Communication bottlenecks and privacy issues are significant challenges for deploying federated training across large-scale distributed systems. This paper presents a novel, privacy-preserving communication protocol for federated training that integrates succinct zero-knowledge proofs with a new sparse update format. By employing this protocol, each client transmits only sparse weight changes to the server accompanied by a concise ZK proof, which certifies both the client's compliance with the training protocol and the privacy of the global model. To ensure practical viability, we provide a comprehensive implementation of this protocol within federated averaging and a variant known as federated averaging with differential privacy. Our approach is evaluated on the FEDERATED learning benchmark using the CIFAR-10 dataset, demonstrating that the proposed protocol achieves communication efficiency gains of up to 90% compared to standard methods.

The diffuse far-ultraviolet (FUV) continuum is widely used to identify the presence of dust within dark clouds. This study investigates the origin of this dust by analyzing FUV continuum data from the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph (COS) on the Hubble Space Telescope, focusing on the Taurus dark cloud complex. We conducted a comprehensive survey of 22 lines of sight, including 10 that penetrate deeply into the cloud core. Our analysis reveals that the observed FUV continuum emission is best explained by the scattering of starlight by small dust grains with sizes less than 0.1 micrometers. These grains are located within the diffuse molecular envelope surrounding the dense core, a region characterized by an enhanced population of small particles. Furthermore, we found that the dust-to-gas ratio in this molecular envelope is comparable to the ratio found in the interstellar medium.

Tables are a standard format for presenting tabular data in academic publications, serving as a compact means to present extensive information. However, tables in existing papers often suffer from poor design, making them difficult to interpret. To address this, we introduce an automated system that generates well-designed table layouts based solely on raw data. Our approach utilizes an evolutionary algorithm to optimize visual designs by applying a domain-specific objective function that evaluates design quality. To support this process, we developed an objective function grounded in the principles of data visualization and data mining. The algorithm operates on a generative framework capable of producing a broad range of possible table structures. Experimental results indicate that this method produces high-quality layouts that effectively apply to various table types.

This work examines the evolution of players' beliefs and their subsequent actions within a multi-stage game characterized by incomplete information. It proposes a novel framework, Dynamic Cognitive Hierarchy Theory, which operates under two key assumptions: first, that each player's strategy is derived from a specific hierarchy of beliefs, and second, that this structure is populated by a diverse range of dynamic cognitive hierarchies. The research investigates the conditions required for the existence and stability of a steady state in this dynamic setting. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that, within a specific parameter range, the resulting steady state aligns with the High-Order Best Response (HOR) distribution of cognitive hierarchies. Consequently, the proposed DCHT offers a distinct alternative to both the standard HOR theory and the fully rational theory, bridging the divide between them.

Accurately gauging a population's size is crucial for setting vaccination policies and planning infrastructure, yet these figures are often obscured by privacy concerns. We present a novel method to estimate population size from the timing of individual events while rigorously safeguarding user privacy. The method's privacy assurance stems from the fact that it does not reveal the count for any single city; instead, it only provides an estimate for the combined total of all cities analyzed. We derive mathematical bounds for the resulting estimation error and validate the approach using simulated data, demonstrating its accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, we apply the method to real-world vaccination data from Germany, yielding a total population estimate of 83.8 million people with a 95% confidence interval ranging from 83.2 million to 84.4 million.

Approximate membership checking (AMC) algorithms are designed to minimize false positives while maintaining a constant query time complexity. This paper introduces several novel filtering architectures to further suppress false positive rates in AMC. New designs include a multi-level Bloom filter (BF) variant, a multi-level BF filter (BF2) for filtering multiple data sets, and a Bloom filter (BF3) for handling single data sets. These methods are evaluated against the BF, Bloom filter (BF), Bloom filter (BF), and Bloom filter (BF) configurations. We investigate the formation of fermionic dimers comprising two fermionic atoms within a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEZC). This process involves two primary mechanisms: (i) the reaction of an evaporatively cooled BEZC with a thermal cloud, where spin-zero atoms pair up via spin-exchange collisions or laser-induced photoassociation to create a fermion pair, and (ii) the conversion of an already bound atom-molecule pair into three zero-spin atoms through inverse processes. We derive a rate equation governing the time evolution of these populations and solve it to determine the steady-state distribution. Our findings indicate that the steady-state ratio of molecules to atom pairs is governed by the scattering lengths of both interactions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the net direction of the dynamical evolution can be controlled by adjusting the relative populations of the BEZC and the thermal cloud.

This study introduces an enhanced multi-resolution smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) approach designed for fluid-structure interactions (FSI). The proposed framework addresses FSI challenges by coupling a multi-resolution SPH fluid domain with a finite element method (FEM) structural domain, employing a weak coupling strategy to facilitate communication between the two solvers. Within the fluid component, we integrate a highly efficient, fully implicit space-time variational SPH formulation. This specific formulation is spatially discretized using the generalized-alpha space-time finite element method, which inherently supports high-resolution multi-resolution capabilities. Furthermore, a consistent space-time mass matrix is constructed to ensure computational efficiency. To maintain stability during interactions, we implement a consistent fluid-force projection technique within the FEM structure solver. The entire methodology is validated through a series of benchmark tests, including a complex scenario featuring a pitching airfoil.

Quantum computing holds significant promise for machine learning, offering the potential to process vast datasets with superior efficiency. This study introduces a quantum-enhanced online learning framework for time series analysis, designed to operate on evolving data streams. We implement a quantum support vector machine (QSVM) within a sliding window architecture to classify time series patterns. We also determine the optimal size for this sliding window by evaluating the model's performance across various configurations. We further investigate the relationship between data window size and quantum kernel parameters, analyzing how they jointly influence accuracy. We evaluate the proposed method using three real-world datasets: stock market data, the ECG heartbeat dataset, and the UCI Energy Regression dataset.

This study evaluates a pitch-shifting technique designed to maintain timbre integrity, which involves splitting speech into glottal source and vocal tract target signals before applying phase-preserving minimum phase prediction to shift the pitch of the source component. The approach was tested on the TTS-Glow model using the LibriSpeech corpus to generate pitch-varied versions. The results indicate that this method effectively retains timbre characteristics, as demonstrated by higher Posterior C-VOWEL scores and lower C-VOWEL error rates compared to pitch-shifted reference audio. Furthermore, these synthesized samples achieved comparable or superior subjective Mean Opinion Scores (MOS) relative to the original recordings.

This study introduces a novel approach to address the challenge of object permanence in video comprehension. Unlike existing models that struggle with unseen objects and entities, our system leverages the principles of object identity, co-occurrence, and interaction, augmented by the prediction of novel objects. This predictive capability allows the proposed model to track existing entities and identify new ones, effectively handling tasks that require multi-step physical common sense. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Video Reasoning Challenge benchmark. Furthermore, the analysis includes visualizations that elucidate the model's reasoning processes.

This study examines the next-to-leading-order (NLO) QCD computation of the cross-section for the neutral-current $\gamma Z$-mediated Drell-Yan process at the LHC, specifically incorporating bottom-quark loop contributions. We present analytical expressions for the relevant coefficient functions and validate our findings against previous numerical evaluations. Additionally, we assess the sensitivity of the process to the strong coupling constant $\alpha_{s}$ and the $\bar{MS}$ mass of the bottom quark, $m_{b}(\bar{MS})$.

Telepresence robots (TPRs) are increasingly adopted to enable remote individuals to traverse unaccessible areas, yet the impact of network performance on remote operator experience remains unexplored. This study investigates how navigation difficulty and TPR movement speed influence Quality of Experience (QoE) across real-time applications. By recruiting 10 participants to perform 100 tasks over 100 minutes using a 5G-connected TPR, the research analyzes the relationships between network metrics, Quality of Service (QoS), and QoE. The findings reveal that QoS metrics are impacted by both network conditions and task complexity, while QoE is further dependent on the operator's TPR speed. Additionally, the data shows that higher speeds result in lower QoE, and more difficult tasks yield even poorer performance. Finally, the study examines the correlation between QoS and QoE, offering a foundational approach for developing future QoE prediction models.

We propose a Bayesian framework for hierarchical regression models that handles both continuous and categorical covariates. In this structure, each level's response is modeled as a linear combination of its corresponding covariates alongside a stochastic error term. We introduce a new class of hierarchical linear models termed the "hierarchical linear threshold model," where level-specific thresholds are assigned independent prior distributions. We develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling algorithm to estimate the posterior distribution of these model parameters. The methodology is demonstrated using two empirical examples: one analyzing count data from a real-world clinical trial and another examining data from a real estate market.

Recent observations of the Kepler-90b system, which revealed 8 planets, have renewed interest in the potential for discovering additional giant worlds. This study investigates how the timing of gas accretion influences the timing of formation and subsequent architecture of giant planet systems. The authors developed a new N-body code, PlanetEsQ, designed to model the formation of giant planets within a protoplanetary disk. The model incorporates the migration of planetesimals and cores, along with the dynamics of gas envelope capture and disk-disk interactions. PlanetEsQ was applied to the Kepler-355 system, yielding a multi-giant system featuring two hot Jupiters, two cold Jupiters, and two gas giants. The resulting configuration closely resembles the system's existing architecture, with all planets possessing masses in the range of 0.1 to 1 Jupiter masses ($M_J$). The study demonstrates that the final structure of a giant system is highly sensitive to the timescales of gas accretion. Specifically, if the accretion duration is shorter than the timescale for migration-induced orbital crossing, planets tend to maintain prograde orbits; conversely, if gas accretion takes longer than this threshold, the planets are likely to undergo orbital crossing and capture into retrograde configurations.

Phonons are essential to the electronic behavior of nanomaterials, yet their interaction with electrons remains difficult to investigate. In this work, we present a technique that correlates changes in electrical conductivity with specific phonon modes, utilizing a nanoscale heater and sensor. This approach allows for the detection of individual phonons, enabling a detailed analysis of their interaction with electrons. The method's effectiveness is validated through experiments on a suspended graphene monolayer, where measured results align well with standard phonon models for such materials. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that a suspended graphene monolayer, when doped with holes and cooled to low temperatures, exhibits strong coupling with optical phonons. This coupling results in a distinct conductivity dip at the phonon resonance temperature, providing direct evidence of their interaction.

This study addresses the unsupervised clustering of high-dimensional data, where features may vary significantly in importance. We introduce a flexible framework that assigns distinct weights to individual features, enabling effective handling of heterogeneous data environments. To achieve this, we present a joint optimization approach for simultaneously determining an optimal clustering structure and the corresponding feature weights. We analyze the theoretical properties of our proposed model and develop a practical algorithm to solve it. Extensive numerical experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate that the method outperforms traditional dimensionality reduction techniques and existing weight learning strategies.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are widely adopted in machine learning for their capacity to represent diverse behaviors and diverse subtasks. However, a primary unresolved issue is the absence of effective tools for identifying relevant experts and their corresponding parameters directly from data. While standard identification methods—such as the EM algorithm, gradient descent, and the Expectation-Maximization approach—have been widely used, they are known to converge slowly or become trapped in local optima when applied to MoE models. To address this, this paper introduces a novel framework that enables simultaneous expert identification and parameter learning. The core of this framework is an algorithm called Expert Relevance Selection (ERS), which integrates an L0-norm penalty into the standard Expectation-Maximization process. By utilizing an iterative strategy, the proposed method can reliably determine the necessary number of experts and accurately estimate their parameters. Furthermore, we establish theoretical guarantees that demonstrate the consistency of our expert selection and parameter estimation procedures under certain conditions. Finally, empirical evaluations on both simulated data and real-world benchmarks confirm that our method outperforms conventional techniques in terms of both computational efficiency and estimation accuracy.

These notes serve as a course introduction to chip-firing games on metric graphs alongside Jacobian and Prym varieties. They are grounded in joint research with Dusa McDuff, noting their relevance to integrable systems, chip-firing games, and Prym varieties of metric graphs.

Recent developments in Lattice QCD have enabled the numerical simulation of scalar and spinor fields possessing mass terms that explicitly break $\mathbb{Z}_2$ global symmetries. This advancement holds significant promise for addressing fundamental questions in both Particle Physics and Cosmology, as these domains frequently rely on such symmetries to establish baryon number conservation and neutrino mass scales. However, the restoration of a $\mathbb{Z}_2}$ symmetry to the QCD vacuum through fermion doublers poses a threat of irreversibility, potentially invalidating the physical interpretations of the aforementioned theories. This review examines the feasibility of applying these lattice techniques across various theoretical frameworks, while also addressing the challenges introduced by the fermion doubling problem.

We have compiled a catalog of blue horizontal branch (BHB) stars in the globular cluster NGC 1846, utilizing data from the Gaia DR2 release. This cluster was previously identified as a potential BHB host by Gaia Collaboration et al. (2018) and has been further scrutinized in this study. Our analysis reveals that the BHB population in NGC 1846 is quite sparse, comprising only 13 stars. This finding aligns with the cluster's intermediate luminosity, which falls between the highest and lowest values observed among known BHB hosts. Additionally, the BHB stars in NGC 1846 exhibit a blue coloration ($0.2 < (BP-RP) < 0.4$), suggesting they possess low helium abundances. This spectral characteristic is consistent with the metal-poor nature of the cluster and mirrors the properties of the blue straggler stars found there. Consequently, NGC 1846 serves as a prime candidate for investigating the evolutionary pathways of blue straggler stars into the blue horizontal branch phase.

This study explores the fundamental group associated with oriented colored broken submersions, building upon the application of the ordered principle to ordered colored graphs. We generalize this approach by applying the $b$-principle to oriented colored broken submersions and construct an entire category based on these concepts. Subsequently, we demonstrate that the fundamental group of this category corresponds exactly to the group of oriented colored broken submersions. Finally, we apply these findings to calculate the fundamental groups for specific categories of ordered and oriented colored graphs and their related structures involving ordered and unoriented colored broken submersions.

The success of transferring knowledge from pre-trained models to new tasks is a well-established fact, yet the factors driving successful transfer or causing degradation in model performance remain poorly understood. This study investigates the transferability of deep neural networks (DNNs) by analyzing the representations they generate. We demonstrate that when a pre-trained network is transferred to a new domain, its high-level features adapt to downstream specifics, while low-level features remain largely preserved. However, our findings also reveal a critical limitation: the inability of pretrained models to fully capture all pre-training domain features at the low-level limits their adaptability to new tasks. Specifically, we observe a strong positive correlation between the similarity of low-level feature distributions and transfer performance. Consequently, our results suggest that enhancing the dissimilarity between distributions prior to training can significantly improve the effectiveness of transferred pre-trained networks.

The structure of a network significantly influences how information propagates within it. While the majority of research has concentrated on the degree of modularity, this study introduces a novel concept termed *network segmentation* to evaluate diffusion efficiency. We propose a segmentation index grounded in the principle that heterogeneous network structures are essential for effective information spread. This approach is validated through a comprehensive analysis of both synthetic and real-world datasets. Furthermore, we conducted extensive simulations using the Independent Cascade (IC) model to demonstrate that the proposed segmentation index correlates strongly with actual information diffusion performance. Ultimately, these findings suggest that network segmentation serves as a superior predictor of diffusion efficiency compared to traditional modularity measures.

The distance between discrete nonlinear interference points (NIs) in the complex plane is utilized to estimate channel memory. This distance is demonstrated to be invariant under rotation and scaling, properties that ensure the distance is preserved across different numerical methods. Specifically, the channel memory can be approximated by dividing this distance by a non-interaction nonlinearity kernel. This kernel is estimated using a regression analysis of interference points derived from channels featuring a channel memory of 51.

A primary obstacle to detecting Android malware is the emergence of problem-space evasion attacks, which render existing detection models ineffective. To counter this, we introduce a new class of solutions termed constraint-aware eaves detection. This framework enables detection models to directly analyze raw binary data while adhering to specific domain constraints. The approach employs variational autoencoders to train detection models capable of incorporating these constraints. Furthermore, we define and develop a novel metric to assess how well a detection model handles various constraints. Experimental results indicate that constraint-aware eaves detection can successfully integrate multiple types of constraints and achieve superior performance in binary classification.

Service-Oriented computing (SOC) has established itself as a foundational element in modern distributed computing, driven by the paradigm of services as atomic units that enable modular construction and reuse. However, the fundamental nature of a service has transitioned from a static static definition based on pre-specified input-output contracts to a dynamic capability offered at a specific moment in time. This temporal shift introduces a critical challenge: the potential divergence between a client's requirements and the actual state of a service, which can lead to execution failures. To address this, the paper proposes a requirement matching mechanism that enforces temporal constraints on both the querying and invocation phases of services. The solution is formalized using a logic built upon temporal logic and directed hypergraphs to model both requirements and services rigorously. The approach is validated through the implementation of a prototype system designed for the identification and resolution of temporal mismatches within telemedicine contexts.

We report on numerical simulations of thermal Hall conductivity in nonchiral top序 matter, focusing on the particle-hole symmetric Pfaffian state. The analysis reveals that the chaotic flux attachment gauge field generates an effective chiral central charge $c_{\rm eff} = -1$, consistent with the state's nonchiral nature. These results offer a reliable method for examining complex top序 phases lacking chiral properties.

This study investigates the physical conditions required for Thakurta black holes to exist within the universe. We present a theoretical model for Thakurta black holes and analyze their stability using the Teukolsky equation. Our analysis demonstrates that these black holes can only form if the universe's temperature drops below approximately $10^{-29}$ Kelvin.

Protoplanetary discs often exhibit pressure maxima, which can facilitate the accumulation of planetesimals and the subsequent growth of planet cores. This study utilizes a new, highly efficient 3D hydrodynamic simulation code to investigate planet formation within pressure-bump environments. We examine two specific cases: a pressure bump created by a migrating planetesimal and one induced by a migrating planet. In both scenarios, the migration rate is set to be significantly slower than the growth timescale of the core. Our findings indicate that if the initial distribution of planetesimals is sufficiently dense, the migrating body can rapidly accrete mass, with accretion rates exceeding $10^{-4} M_{\oplus}/yr$. Additionally, the resulting planet exhibits a mass profile skewed toward the trailing edge of the pressure bump. These outcomes suggest that planetesimals trapped in pressure bumps are prone to swift consumption by migrating cores, potentially explaining the scarcity of such planeteseals observed today.

This paper introduces a novel learning theory framework that links the theoretical requirements for computational ease with the number of model parameters. We establish an algorithm capable of learning a specific neural architecture within $\tilde{O}(d^2)$ time using $\tilde{O}(d^2)$ parameters to achieve an empirical loss of $\epsilon$ on an $\epsilon$-hard dataset containing $n$ samples. Our results demonstrate that the parameter count grows only polynomially with respect to the dimension $d$ and the inverse square root of $\epsilon$, whereas the leading time complexity for standard gradient descent scales with the square root of $\epsilon$. These findings suggest a significant advantage in training efficiency. Additionally, we prove a lower bound indicating that the proposed parameter complexity is nearly optimal.

In a counterexample to a question posed by Tao, we provide evidence showing that for every $r\geq 2$, a set $A$ within a countable discrete abelian group $G$ containing a Bohr set $B$ within $A+A$ does not necessarily mean $A$ itself contains a (smaller) Bohr set $B'$ such that $rB'\subseteq A$. However, we demonstrate that such a $B'$ with $rB'\subseteq A$ does exist under the specific condition that $G$ is virtually divisible.

Ridepooling has emerged as a cost-effective and sustainable urban transport option, prompting providers to focus on enhancing service quality and profitability through increased ride-sharing. This study addresses the trade-off between pooling rates and minimizing passenger detours by proposing a novel approach that allows users to voluntarily accept specific, predefined maximum waiting times or maximum detour limits. We introduce a new algorithm based on a modified Vehicle Routing Problem with Time Windows (VRPTW) to optimally assign shared rides within these time constraints. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques, yielding significant improvements in both pooling rates and customer travel times.

The rising popularity of digital shopping has led to an exponential increase in the generation of multi-modal data within e-commerce environments. However, this data often suffers from inherent issues such as missing values, noise, and imbalances. To address these challenges, researchers have developed various data fusion and completion methods for multi-modal datasets. Yet, a critical limitation remains: most existing approaches fail to account for the correlations between different data modes. To resolve this, we introduce a novel Multi-Mode Correlation Completion (MMCC) method. By leveraging correlations across modes, MMCC effectively handles multi-mode incomplete datasets. To validate the approach, we conducted experiments on three real-world datasets and compared the results against several state-of-the-art methods. The empirical analysis demonstrates that MMCC outperments these benchmarks in terms of effectiveness.

Deep InfoMax (DIM) represents a pioneering unsupervised deep learning technique that surpasses traditional methods in detecting abnormalities within brain imaging. This study evaluates DIM's performance against the widely used in silico radiomics (ISG-R) model, which relies on conventional radiomic features, specifically examining their efficacy in identifying Alzheimer's disease (AD) and distinguishing AD from mild cognitive impairment (MCI). The analysis reveals that DIM outperforms ISG-R in both AD and AD/MCI classification tasks. Furthermore, DIM exhibits a higher concordance with established neuropathological AD findings and demonstrates superior stability regarding test-retest reliability. These results suggest that DIM holds significant potential for enhancing brain imaging analysis.

This paper presents I-score, a novel interpretability-driven metric for text classification that operates by measuring a token's influence on a model's output. By ranking tokens based on their significance, I-score provides interpretability and can simultaneously identify important tokens for downstream applications. Empirical evaluations conducted on various text classification benchmarks demonstrate that I-score surpasses existing interpretability metrics in accuracy. Furthermore, integrating I-score into a re-clasification strategy yields state-of-the-art results on both single- and multi-label tasks. Finally, we verify I-score's utility in explaining factual queries and generating summaries, with comparative analysis against current explanation methods.

We investigate the spin-orbit coupling (SOC) within a two-orbital Hubbard model featuring nearest-neighbor coupling, focusing on the paramagnetic phase. By employing exact diagonalization and cluster mean-field theories, we examine the paramagnetic ground state's dependence on interaction strength ($U$) and orbital overlap ($t_{12}$). Our findings reveal that the effective $\lambda_{\rm eff}$ scales linearly with intrinsic $\lambda$ at weak interactions but diminishes as $t_{\rm eff}$ approaches zero under strong electron correlations. Consequently, a paramagnetic state characterized by a vanishing, or "soft," spin-orbit coupling emerges in the Mott limit. These results underscore the critical role of electron interactions in modulating spin-orbit effects, with significant implications for systems such as twisted bilayer graphene and twisted bilayer $t$-PNH.

We investigate a simple model featuring a "simple" $U(1)$ gauge symmetry that is broken by a complex scalar field, which also carries a charge under a global $U(1)_R$ symmetry. This setup generates a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson (pNGB) that is protected from acquiring mass through the standard $U(1)_R$ charge, allowing it to serve as a viable dark matter candidate. Although the mechanism protecting this dark matter mass is robust, the associated long-lived nature of the particle can be compromised by higher-dimensional operators. Specifically, particles with masses comparable to that of the universe's age are considered to be very long-lived, while lighter ones decay within cosmological timescales. The model's parameters are constrained by existing experimental data, including direct detection limits, the observed relic density of dark matter, and cosmological bounds on extra relativistic degrees of freedom.

Assessing the performance of AI-driven medical devices regarding distribution drifts is critical for their practical deployment. However, the inherent complexity of medical datasets and the restricted availability of labeled data have impeded the development of robust evaluation methodologies. This study introduces a framework to bridge that gap by reinterpreting the generalization error in medical AI as an out-of-domain (OOD) prediction challenge. Leveraging techniques from unsupervised domain adaptation, the framework enables the estimation of expected performance on OOD data using only in-domain examples. By redefining data distribution shifts as shifts in the input space, the approach eliminates the need for additional labeled medical data. Empirical evaluations utilizing two public datasets for medical image segmentation and three regression tasks confirm that the framework accurately gauges generalization errors. Furthermore, it successfully identifies specific regions within the input space that exhibit elevated prediction errors, thereby revealing characteristics of the shift.

This study introduces a novel force field switching function designed to facilitate a seamless transition between bonded and non-bounded interactions in nucleic acid simulations. By enabling all-atom simulations with explicit solvent, the method supports the control of all six rotational degrees of freedom, including tilt, roll, twist, buckle, propeller twist, and opening. Validation through simulations of an A-DNA unit cell solvated in water demonstrates that structural characteristics and dynamic behaviors align well with experimental data and existing literature. Furthermore, the approach was applied to an expanded system comprising four DNA quadruplexes in liquid water, showing that the results are consistent with experimental data and computational predictions.

Duda's Asymmetric Numeral Systems (ANS) is a universal lossless encoder that achieves near-theoretical minimum redundancy. While a variant utilizing precise initialization, known as tANS, was previously shown to produce a 0.14-bit-per-symbol overhead, this study introduces a new tANS variation that reduces redundancy encoding to only 0.07 bits per symbol. We validate these findings through experiments on standard benchmarks, achieving a speed of 3.6 GB/s with a 0.7-bit per symbol loss in redundancy compared to the previous 0.14-bit baseline.

This study presents a dielectric theory for electrolytes that explicitly accounts for ion interactions. Building upon the classical Debye-Hückel framework, which treats ions as non-interacting point particles, we incorporate interactions by modeling ions as hard spheres. Within this approach, we calculate the dielectric constant of the electrolyte liquid by analyzing the total dipole moments of individual ions alongside their spatial distribution. We further decompose the dielectric constant into two components: the dielectric of the pure solvent and an additional term arising from ionic contributions. We analyze how increasing ionic strength diminishes the dielectric constant through two mechanisms: the formation of ion pairs, which reduces the number of effective dipoles, and ion clustering, which suppresses the orientational mobility of the solvent.

We analyze a spectrum of hadrons composed of heavy quark-antiquark pairs, specifically heavy-baryon-heavy-antibaryon systems. Our study focuses on interactions between spin-1/2 pentaquarks and spin-0 or spin-1 hexapquarks (such as $\Xi_c^{--}$ or $\Omega_c^{*}$) and their corresponding antiparticles, such as $\Omega_c^{*}\Omega_c^{*}$ or $\Xi_c^{*}\Xi_c^{*}$. By applying a variational method, we determine the mass spectra of these hadronic molecules. The resulting predicted masses align closely with the observed resonance peaks of $\Omega_c^{*}\Omega_c^{*}\approx 6.9$ GeV, $\Xi_c^{*}\Xi_c^{*}\approx 7.3$ GeV, $\Xi_c^{*}\Omega_c^{*}\approx 7.3$ GeV, and $\Xi_c^{*}\Xi_c^{*}\approx 7.3$ GeV. These findings suggest that the resonances $\Omega_c^{*}\Omega_c^{*}\approx 6.9$ GeV, $\Xi_c^{*}\Xi_c^{*}\approx 7.3$ GeV, $\Xi_c^{*}\Xi_c^{*}\approx 7.3$ GeV, and $\Xi_c^{*}\Xi_c^{*}\approx

Military drones have garnered significant attention from researchers, scholars, and the general public, with a marked increase in related work published in 2019 and 2020. However, this research activity was severely disrupted by the global pandemic, causing a notable decline in publications during 2021. This paper introduces a comprehensive survey of military drone swarms, covering their fundamental concepts, operational environments, and key design challenges. The survey analyzes 2019 and 2021 publications from the IEEE Xplore, Springer, and ACM repositories, which were selected based on specific inclusion and exclusion criteria. The paper systematically examines the identified studies across four primary domains: mission types, communication methods, attack strategies, and defense methods. Additionally, it explores the potential of integrating machine learning and reinforcement learning to enhance swarm behavior and performance.

We introduce a new method for computing the three-dimensional Ly-$\alpha$ correlation function, utilizing a hybrid approach that combines a machine learning model with a semi-analytical framework. This method is benchmarked against $N$-body simulations, demonstrating that it accurately reproduces the correlation function across all scales. We apply this technique to re-examine the constraints on cosmological parameters derived from the BOSS eBOSS sample, which encompasses the quasar samples CMASS and eClvO. Our findings indicate that incorporating the complete correlation function shape improves constraints on these parameters by approximately 10% compared to analyses using only the Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) peak. Additionally, we find that including the full correlation function yields a 20% improvement in parameter constraints over models that account for the full two-dimensional correlation function.

In the field of High Energy Physics, the exchange of emittance between horizontal and vertical planes is a critical factor, particularly for modern circular electron storage rings designed to achieve ultra-low emittance. This study presents a new analytical method for determining the dynamic emittance exchange between horizontal and vertical planes in continuous linear motion. The analysis relies on the Courant-Snyder invariant and demonstrates that dynamic emittance exchange can occur even when the standard Twiss parameters remain constant. This phenomenon is attributed to the continuous variation of the relative emittance ratio during the motion. Consequently, dynamic emittance growth may occur even in ideal theoretical conditions where no actual forces act upon the particle beam.

Pedestrian trajectory prediction is a crucial component of autonomous driving, crowd management, and wearable assistive devices for the visually impaired. However, forecasting future paths remains challenging due to the complex and varied intentions behind human movement. This study introduces a new deep learning approach for pedestrian trajectory prediction that effectively captures both short-term and long-term temporal dependencies. The proposed method combines Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to extract high-level features from movement patterns. Specifically, the architecture utilizes an attention-enhanced CNN-LSTM (AE-CNN-LSTM) model that first processes the entire trajectory as input data. The attention mechanism allows the system to weigh different segments of the path, identifying the most significant parts for predicting subsequent movements. The LSTM component then forecasts the trajectory based on these attention-driven features. Experimental results demonstrate that the AE-CNN-LSTM model outperforms existing methods in accuracy. The source code and datasets are accessible at https://github.com/Anubhav-1/AE-CNN-LSTM-Pedestrian-Path-Prediction.

This study investigates how the temporal sequence of Hebbian weight updates influences emergent complexity in a single-layer discrete-time recurrent neural network. Specifically, we examine how the time-averaged complexity of a network with a fixed fixed-point attractor responds to learning rates and the type of input data, utilizing a measure based on the Lyapunov exponent. Findings indicate that incremental, incremental Hebbian rules promote higher complexity, whereas competitive Hebbian rules lead to lower complexity. Additionally, we demonstrate that the complexity of a network exposed to natural data from a source can match that of a network trained on that same data. Finally, we show that the complex dynamics of a network without constraints can be replicated in a network with a fixed fixed-point attractor by adjusting the fixed-point's value and applying a suitable scaling factor to the weights.

We present a new approach for modifying the collective dynamics of multi-robot systems through human hand gestures. This technique integrates human intent into robot behavior by merging non-intrusive magnetic fields with the non-holonomic constraints of unmarked, commercially available robots. The system features a neural network that interprets hand gestures to adjust the strength of these magnetic fields, enabling direct robot-to-human communication. This communication channel allows individual robot behaviors to respond dynamically to human inputs while maintaining their inherent swarm intelligence. Experimental results demonstrate that this magnetic field modulation effectively alters robot speed and inter-robot distances, facilitating efficient transmission of human gestures and their semantic meaning.

Automated white blood cell classification is vital for medical diagnostics, a need increasingly addressed by machine learning. This study presents an accessible implementation of the YOLOv4 neural network for YOLOv4, which processes blood cell images to derive classification results. This code serves as a foundational element for a broader system designed to analyze and diagnose blood samples.

Counterdiabatic protocols offer an optimal framework for rapidly transitioning between quantum states without traversing intermediate levels. This study introduces a novel protocol for preparing molecular ground states efficiently and adiabatically-like by counterdiabatic techniques. The required time-dependent control field is derived using a two-step strategy: first, a zeroth-order approximation is established via a generalized Bloch function; second, corrections are applied by treating molecular vibrations as a perturbation. The resulting control expression is validated against two specific cases: a hydrogen molecule in an electric field and a nitrogen molecule in a magnetic field. Furthermore, the performance of this quantum algorithm is benchmarked against standard adiabatic protocols. The comparison demonstrates that the proposed method significantly reduces exposure to non-resonant excitations, thereby lowering the probability of transitions to excited states.

Grayscale images are extensively utilized in various image processing domains, including biometrics, medical imaging, and remote sensing. Nevertheless, existing techniques for restoring noise and contrast in these images often rely on the assumption of a uniform distribution, an idealization that frequently fails to hold true for practical applications. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel model that incorporates both a general distribution and a data-fidelity term to enhance the accuracy of our approach. We further develop an efficient iterative algorithm based on the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to solve the proposed model. The convergence of this method is rigorously established, and its practical performance is validated through numerical experiments on real-world image datasets.

We establish that any differentiable function taking complex values and depending on real variables can be represented, within any arbitrary epsilon-precision, as a sum of exponentials containing at most N+1 distinct exponents, where N represents the complex function's degree of smoothness. This result serves as an approximation for such functions, forming the basis of an exact identity valid in any arbitrary precision. This exact identity serves as an initial step toward quantizing Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formalisms. By applying these formalisms within an arithmetic framework, one obtains equations of motion that remain invariant under time discretization. Consequently, one can derive Hamiltonians expressed as sums of exponentials having far fewer distinct exponents than the function originally required to approximate them. This phenomenon mirrors the concept of exact solution invariance found in classical integrable systems. Furthermore, this reduction in the number of distinct exponents in the Hamiltonian may be interpreted as a form of quantum integrability. Finally, this approach enables the arithmetical quantization of any phase space, resulting in a reduced dimensionality characterized by fewer distinct exponents in the resulting Hamiltonian.

This study examines the challenge of exchanging Relational to RDF data, focusing specifically on target frameworks that employ typed IRI (Typed IRIs) constructs. We demonstrate that TysRDF (Typed IRIs in RDF) offers a more expressive power than the untyped IRIs construct, rendering it a more suitable solution for various data exchange scenarios. Furthermore, we establish that the challenge of full dependency preservation for TysRDF is undecidable. Conversely, we identify sufficient conditions ensuring that any fully dependency-preserving TysRDF solution can be effectively generated. Finally, we explore the feasibility of achieving partial dependency preservation and prove that this specific problem is also undecidable.

This study introduces new techniques for measuring progress, technical efficiency, and potential output expansion in production and consumption contexts, building upon recent developments in flexible regression techniques. The authors present a panel data framework for joint estimating the stochastic production frontier and the underlying distance function. Additionally, they propose a nonlinear dynamic translog production function to allow for time-varying output elasticities alongside a flexible stochastic frontier model. The resulting dynamic panel data technique is implemented using the generalized method of moments (GMM). Empirical findings, based on data from 100 listed Chinese banks between 2007 and 2016, reveal that the average efficiency score has been declining over time. The analysis also finds substantial potential for output growth, alongside a negative correlation between efficiency scores and output variability.

This study examines the low-mass scalar pair production process ($pp \to \Phi\Phi \to 4b$) at the LHC, specifically targeting scenarios where the mass is below 500 GeV. We propose a reconstruction technique utilizing a machine-learning-based tagger for scalar decays into $b\bar{b}$ $j$-jets. We further demonstrate that, for processes of interest, this approach yields a mass resolution improvement of 1.5 to 2.5 times compared to standard methods. Consequently, we find that the sensitivity to light scalar production can be enhanced by a factor of 1.5 to 2.5, even when integrating a luminosity of 300 $\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$.
